source.version: WRONG DOCUMENT ON FILE. The file is the arXiv preprint 2303.12003 (PDF metadata: 'GAIvsHumans_preprint.docx', created 2023-03-21) of Haase and Hanel, 'Artificial muses'. It is not the c493 record, which is the AEA RCT Registry entry AEARCTR-0016306 by Mir Djawadi and Fahr (first posted 2025-06-30, no linked paper). The retrieval matched on title via an arXiv title search.
source.title_on_document: Artificial muses: Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots Have Risen to Human-Level Creativity

supplement.where: Referred to as 'supplemental materials'; no URL given for it. Data and R code at https://osf.io/9fctd/?view_only=6c8f02c6972b49319c12f87cfb3f76db
supplement.holds: Table S1 (intraclass correlations by prompt), Figures S1 and S2 (AI-rated originality), and all fluency results

paper_design_summary: This summary describes the document on file, which is a different paper from the c493 registry record. 100 Prolific participants (US, native English speakers) completed the Alternative Uses Test for five objects without any AI. The authors also prompted five generative-AI chatbots (alpa.ai, Copy.ai, ChatGPT-3, AI21 Studio, YouChat), and later GPT-4, with the same five objects. Six blind human raters and an AUT-trained language model scored the originality of every response, and the paper compares human with chatbot originality and fluency.

studies.label: Alternative Uses Test: 100 humans vs. generative-AI chatbots (Haase and Hanel; document on file, not the c493 registration)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned between AI and no AI. All human participants worked without AI; chatbot responses were generated by the authors. Only the order of the five prompts was randomized.
assignment.quote: we compared the creativity of GAI chatbots with humans: We applied the Alternative Uses Test (AUT28) to 100 human participants and five GAI.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 2 Results; p. 12, Materials ('The order in which the prompts were presented was randomized')

arms.name: Humans
arms.description: Prolific participants writing alternative uses for five objects, three minutes per object, no AI

arms.name: GAI chatbots
arms.description: Five chatbots (alpa.ai, Copy.ai, ChatGPT-3, AI21 Studio, YouChat) prompted 'What can you do with [prompt]?' with up to three 'What else?' follow-ups; GPT-4 added later and rated only by the AI scorer

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions stated. Non-answers and unrelated answers were excluded at the response level for humans and chatbots.
participants.who: Prolific Academic participants, native English speakers with full- or part-time work; M age = 41.00 (SD = 12.25); 50 women, 50 men
participants.quote: In total, 100 participants completed our study (Mage = 41.00, SD = 12.25, 50 women, 50 men), who were recruited through Prolific Academic.

ai_tool.name_model: alpa.ai, Copy.ai (freestyle template), ChatGPT (GPT-3), AI21 Studio (Jurassic-1, Playground), YouChat; GPT-4 in follow-up
ai_tool.how_used: AI produced its own AUT responses for comparison with human responses; no person used AI.

task.description: Alternative Uses Test for five objects: ball, fork, pants, tire, tooth(brush)
task.duration: Three minutes per object for humans; average completion time 17 minutes

outcomes.name: Originality rated by six human raters (CAT, 1-5 scale), averaged per creator and prompt
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Six raters blind to the source, consensual assessment technique, 1-5 scale; ICCs .85 to .94. Analyzed by a linear mixed model with random intercepts and slopes for prompts, and by per-prompt between-subject t-tests.

outcomes.name: Originality scored by an AUT-trained language model
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Trained LLM for AUT scoring (Organisciak et al. 2022); correlates with mean human rating rs = .78 to .94. Also the only score for GPT-4 (follow-up: on average 9.4 humans more original than GPT-4 across prompts).

contrasts.locator: p. 4, Originality; p. 5, Table 1; p. 7, GPT-4

outcomes.name: Fluency (number of ideas)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Sum of ideas per participant or chatbot as counted by the AI and each of the six raters. Full results only in the supplement.

contrasts.reported: Main text only: 'the GAI chatbots came up with 2-3 times more ideas than humans.' Statistics in the supplement, not in this PDF.

eligibility.reason: The document on file (Haase and Hanel 2023, arXiv 2303.12003) compares AI-generated with human-generated AUT responses; no person received AI help, so it is ai_vs_human context evidence (100 humans vs. five chatbots). It is NOT the c493 record. c493 is the AEA RCT Registry entry AEARCTR-0016306 (Mir Djawadi and Fahr), a registration with no results and no linked paper, so its eligibility cannot be judged from a results document. The Haase and Hanel paper should be screened under its own cid if it is not already in the candidate list.

one_line_finding: Document on file (Haase and Hanel, not c493): human- and AI-rated originality of 100 humans' AUT ideas did not differ from five chatbots' ideas (mixed models B = -0.21, SE = 0.15, p = .218 and B = -0.18, SE = 0.13, p = .241; p. 4, Table 1 p. 5).
open_questions: Retrieval error: the file for c493 is Haase and Hanel (2023), 'Artificial muses', arXiv 2303.12003, not the Mir Djawadi and Fahr registration AEARCTR-0016306. Re-retrieve c493 from https://www.socialscienceregistry.org/trials/16306, or mark it as a registration with no results.
Check whether Haase and Hanel (2023) already has its own cid; if not, add it as an ai_vs_human context paper.

The c493 candidate record describes a planned randomized design (no AI vs. generative-AI assistance with preselected or free prompts; matchstick-figure task; 50-70 adults and 50-70 children per arm). Nothing in the file on hand confirms this.
notes: Criterion 2 is marked unclear because the 100 people analyzed in the file on hand never received AI, so the count does not apply to an AI-assignment contrast. Per-prompt t-tests compare 100 humans with 5 chatbots (unequal samples noted by the authors, p. 4). Count of humans more original than the best chatbot: 32.8 on average across prompts (p. 4) and 9.4 against GPT-4 (p. 7). Comparisons among the five chatbots appear in Figure 2 and Figure S2 only (p. 5, p. 7).
